Title: Playing Dice with the Universe: Programming Quantum Computers to Play Traditional Games
Text:
Playing Dice with the Universe: Programming
Quantum Computers to Play Traditional Games
Tristan Zaborniak
Department of Computer Science
University of Victoria
Victoria, BC, Canada
tristanz@uvic.ca
Vikram Khipple Mulligan
Center for Computational Biology
Flatiron Institute
New York, NY, United States of America
vmulligan@flatironinstitute.org
Abstract—The challenge of programming classical computers
to play traditional, competitive games against human players has
helped to advance classical hardware and software. Quantum
computers have the potential to play games in a unique way:
programmed only with the rules of a game, they should be able
to implicitly represent all future paths of a game leading to wins,
losses, or draws, and sample from this path set to identify moves
that maximize the likelihood of a win. This permits skilled play
without hard-coded or machine-learned strategy. As a proof of
principle, we present early results obtained after programming
the D-Wave quantum annealer with the rules of tic-tac-toe,
enabling it to play against a human opponent. We anticipate
that, as it has for classical computers, game-playing will serve as
an important real-world benchmark for quantum computers.
Index Terms—quantum annealing, games, tic-tac-toe, noughts
and crosses, game theory
I. INTRODUCTION
Quantum computing has incredible potential for solving
currently-intractable optimization problems underlying chal-
lenges in biology, chemistry, physics, and engineering. In past
work, we have demonstrated applications in peptide design
[1] and in molecular docking [2]. However, advancement of
the field suffers since many applications seem esoteric to
laypeople.
Classical computing once suffered the same problem. A
turning point came in 1950, when University of Toronto
graduate student Joseph Kates introduced “Bertie the Brain” at
the Canadian National Exhibition (CNE). “Bertie” was the first
computer to play a well-known game, tic-tac-toe, serving as an
easily understandable way to introduce laypeople to classical
computers’ potential to perform tasks involving complicated
reasoning. Although popular with CNE crowds, the paradigm-
shifting significance of “Bertie” was not recognized at the
time, warranting only the briefest of mentions in a Toronto
Star humour column [3].
Three years later, in 1953, Alan Turing published a specu-
lative article about the potential for computers to play chess
[4]. By 1955, machine learning (ML) allowed computers
to play checkers [5], launching serious attempts to develop
skilful game-playing computers. By 1996, IBM’s specialized
Deep Blue computer was able to beat grandmaster Garry
Kasparov in chess [6], and in 2016, Google’s AlphaGo neural
net, running on widely-available cloud computing hardware,
defeated Go grandmaster Lee Sedol [7] — a major milestone
in the current deep learning renaissance.
As a side-effect of research into developing game-playing
computers, games involving play against computer opponents
have become common pastimes, and this fuelled the rise of
consumer graphics processing units (GPUs), which in turn
proved invaluable for scientific computing and deep learning.
Thus, over the last 76 years, the task of programming classical
computers to play games has propelled both methodological
advancements in classical computing and public engagement
with classical computers, with myriad unanticipated benefits.
Specialized quantum games, with gameplay that incorpo-
rates the concepts of superposition, entanglement, and mea-
surement triggering wavefunction collapse, have been created
to teach humans about quantum mechanics and quantum
computing [8]. Quantum algorithms also exist to solve single-
player puzzles such as Sudoku [9]. However, the authors are
not aware of major forays into developing quantum algorithms
to play traditional, competitive games. Taking, for example,
chess and Go, whose decision trees are astronomically vast,
there is potential for quantum advantage, given that quantum
computers has been shown to offer advantages over classical
computers for solving hard combinatorial problems in princi-
ple [10], [11] and in practice [12], [13].
Classical computers have a well-defined state at every point
in a calculation, even when operating in parallel, limiting
them to explicit consideration of a relatively small number of
possible future paths of a game at a time. As a result, classical
game-playing is largely limited to some combination of exe-
cuting fixed algorithms with hard-coded strategies for winning
a particular game, or using ML-based study of past instances
of a particular game to determine future gameplay. Quantum
computers, by contrast, may exist in superpositions of astro-
nomically many states, permitting implicit representation of
the full decision tree from a given game state. A quantum
computer programmed only with the rules and objective of a
game can, in principle, sample next moves preferentially from
paths that maximize win probability without prior knowledge
of optimal strategy or typical gameplay.
To explore this idea, we programmed the D-Wave Ad-
vantage quantum annealer to play tic-tac-toe. While this is
a task mastered by classical computers 76 years ago, we

constrained ourselves to providing the quantum annealer with
only information about the rules of gameplay and the objective
(the win conditions), excluding any information about strategy
beyond the assumption that a player with a win available on
their move would make the move yielding that win (a general
assumption for competitive games of complete information).
Although this is a very early foray into developing game-
playing algorithms for quantum computers, we demonstrate
a working tic-tac-toe playing quantum algorithm executing on
current hardware, the D-Wave Advantage 2 quantum annealer,
and show that it is able to win consistently against a randomly-
playing opponent. We discuss preliminary findings, potential
avenues for improvement, and generalization to other compet-
itive games of complete or incomplete information.
II. METHODS
In order to model the entire space of future moves of a game
from a given current state, a quantum computer’s state space
must be at least as large as the game’s state space. Tic-tac-
toe is a convenient proof of principle, since (ignoring board
symmetry) there are at most 9! = 362, 880 possible games.
Thus, 19 qubits (yielding a state space of 524,288 states) are
needed at a minimum. In practice, many games lead to a win
before the board is filled, so there are actually only 255,168
possible games [14]. This means that a very clever algorithm
might shave off one qubit; however, we do not seek to be that
miserly with our qubits, or that clever.
We chose to carry out our quantum computations with the
D-Wave quantum annealer for a proof of principle due to the
optimization-like nature of the problem of sampling from a
desired distribution of game states, and due to the maturity
of the D-Wave hardware; however, our approach could also
be used with gate-based hardware and with corresponding
strategies for optimization or ground state sampling, such as
the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) [15]
or quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) [16].
Since a game of tic-tac-toe can at most be nine moves long,
we define at most nine registers, each representing one move,
of nine qubits each. These “move registers” will represent
all possible games of tic-tac-toe using a one-hot encoding
indicating the position filled by an X or an O in a given move.
As the game progresses, the setup will be altered so that the
superposition of states represents the subset of possible games
that are compatible with the current state of play. Qubits in
the “move registers” will be designated mi,x,y where i ∈[1, 9]
represents the move index and x ∈[1, 3] and y ∈[1, 3]
are the coordinates of the grid cell. We also define a “line
register” of five qubits, designated li, with i ∈[5, 9]. These
are used to detect the presence of three of the same symbol
in a row on the ith move. (Note that it is not possible to
have three in a row before the fifth move). A five-qubit “no-
line register”, designated ni, complements the line register by
ensuring that line register qubits remain in the 0 state when no
line of three is completed on a given turn. We also designate
a three-qubit “existing-line register”. These qubits, designated
ei for i ∈[7, 9], are used to indicate that at least one previous

An AND (i1, i2, o, pAND) gate couples three qubits (inputs i1
and i2; output o) using a penalty pAND, yielding the overall
penalty values given in Table Ia. Like a classical AND gate,
the degenerate ground state (bold in Table Ia) includes all
states in which at least one input is 0 and the output is 0, and
the state in which both inputs are 1 and the output is 1. This
is accomplished by adding pAND to Ji1,i2, adding 3pAND to ho,
and adding −2pAND to each of Ji1,o and Ji2,o.

An OR (i1, i2, o, pOR) gate may be created by setting:
hi1 = hi2 = ho = Ji1,i2 = pOR, and
Ji1,o = Ji2,o = −2pOR

D. Defining a WAND (“weak AND”) gate
We also define a WAND (i1, i2, a, o, pWAND) gate (or “weak
AND” gate), which couples two input qubits, i1 and i2, an
ancillary qubit a, and an output qubit o using a penalty pWAND.
In the degenerate ground state (bold in Table IIIa), o is 1 if
both i1 and i2 are 1, but o can be either 0 or 1 if either or
both of i1 and i2 are 0. We call this “WAND” since its penalty
value table resembles, but is distinct from, the truth table for
a classical AND gate. In the WAND case, the output is always
1 if the two inputs are 1, but may or may not be 0 otherwise,
depending on other couplings. We accomplish this by starting
with an AND (i1, i2, a, pWAND) gate (subsection II-A), ensuring
that in the ground state, a is 1 if and only if i1 and i2 are
both 1. We then couple a and o to ensure that (a, o) = (1, 0)
is penalized, and all other states have energy 0. We do this by
adding pWAND to the bias ha for a, and −pWAND to the coupling
Ja,o between a and o.
E. Defining a PW (“past win”) gate
We define a fifth gate called PW (i1, i2, o1, o2, pPW), for
ensuring that past wins prevent future instances of three
characters in a row from registering as a win. Its penalty values
are shown in Table IIIb, and are configured by setting:
hi1 = hi2 = ho1 = ho2 = Jo1,o2 = Ji1,o2 = pPW,
Ji1,o1 = Ji2,o2 = −2pPW, and
Ji1,i2 = Ji2,o1 = −pPW.
If any of these biases or couplings has already been set, we
add to them.
F. Programming allowed moves into the Hamiltonian
Our first goal was to set biases and couplings to construct a
highly degenerate ground state in which bitstrings correspond-
ing to possible allowed games of tic-tac-toe are isoenergetic
and lowest-energy, and all other bitstrings are excited states.
Specifically, we encoded the following rules:
1) Exactly one square must be marked per move. This
necessitates a positive multi-selection penalty pms to
be added to the couplings for all pairs of qubits
(mi,x,y, mi,x′,y′) ∀(x, y) ̸= (x′, y′) in each move
register i, and a bonus of −pms
2 to be added to all biases
for each qubit mi,x,y∀(x, y) in each move register i.
2) The same square may not be marked twice. This requires
a positive overlap penalty po to be added to the couplings
for every pair of qubits (mi,x,y, mj,x,y) ∀i ̸= j, and a
bonus −po
2 to be added to each bias for each qubit mi,x,y.
3) Moves that have been made remain in place and reduce
the state space. When programming the annealer for a
mid-game move n > i, if an X or O has been placed in
a square (x, y) on move i, then a positive penalty of po
is added to the biases of all qubits mj,x,y ∀i ̸= j to
ensure that the ground state does not include any move
that marks that square again. This shrinks the ground state
to the superposition of possible games remaining.
Once these values are added to the biases and couplings for
the move registers, repeated sampling of the ground state
will produce a series of bitstrings each representing a single
possible future path of the game given only the valid moves.
The bitstrings represent the square marked in each move,
expressed as a one-hot encoding in each move register. Note
that we do not need to represent whether a square is occupied
by an X or an O, since this may be inferred from the move
history: a square marked on an odd move contains an X, and
one marked on an even move contains an O.
G. Programming the objective into the Hamiltonian
Unbiased sampling from the ground state of the Hamiltonian
established thus far should result in all possible games being
sampled with equal probability — a task already difficult to
achieve classically without introducing bias. It is advantageous
to be able to sample selectively from those game paths leading
to a win, loss, or draw, however, to allow paths to wins to be
sampled from even when rare. To this end, we next sought to
encode a concept of winning or losing, to implicitly permit
efficient sampling from the subset of game paths that result
in a win for X, or the subset that result in a win for O.
We also sought to ensure that we limited the game paths to
3


the subset in which players presented with a winning move
always embraced that move (minimally strategic play). For
this purpose, we aimed to program the line register qubits so
that the ground state would encode a 1 if a given move resulted
in a win for that player, and a 0 otherwise. To accomplish this,
we encoded the following rules:
4) Three X markings or three O markings in a row, in a
column, or along a diagonal amount to a win. We note
that a win is not possible before the fifth move of a tic-tac-
toe game. Thus, for each qubit representing square (x, y)
in move register i ≥5, we add a series of WAND gates
with coupling strength pline. Each couples input qubits
mj,x1,y1 and mi−2,x2,y2 to output qubit mi,x,y, with one
such gate for each pair ((x1, y1) , (x2, y2)) that could
complete a row, column, or diagonal with (x, y), and
for each j < (i −2) |j mod 2 = i mod 2. Additionally,
the ancilla qubit from each of these WAND gates and
the output qubit mi,x,y are the input to another WAND,
also with strength pline, that connects to output line qubit
li. The effect is to ensure that on the move that a row,
column, or diagonal is filled, the line qubit for that move
is set to 1. To ensure that the line qubit is zero in the
absence of a line of three completed on move i, we anti-
constrain line qubit li and no-line qubit ni with a positive
coupling pnoline. We ensure that no-line qubit ni is 1 if
there is no line completed on move i by applying a WNOT
gate coupling each ancilla qubit from the second set of
WAND gates for the win qubit to the no-win qubit.
5) A player who is able to win on a given move will do so
(minimally strategic play). Effectively, this is encoded in
the implementation of the previous rule, by not adding
win checks for all possible ways of winning in a row,
column, or diagonal. Because two of the moves consid-
ered are moves i and i−2, the win condition requires that
the second X or O that can be involved in the win must
be placed two moves (one turn for the winning player)
before the third X or O involved in the win. This means
that a game path in which an available win is not taken is
an excited state, excluded from the ground state ensemble.
Note that this could be extended to any assumptions
that one wished to encode about one’s opponent’s play;
however, in the case of tic-tac-toe, encoding too many
assumptions about the opponent’s play could yield an
emergent strategy that approaches the Nash equilibrium,
which inevitably results in a draw [17].
6) Only the first three-in-a-row is a win. To this point,
we ensure that three of the same symbol in a row
triggers a 1 in the line qubit for the move on which
the third was placed; however, there is no notion that
the game stops at this point. We must now couple the
line qubits with the win qubits to ensure that a win is
only registered on the first move that produces three
in a row. To this end, we first apply OR (l5, l6, e7, pex),
OR (l7, e7, e8, pex), and OR (l8, e8, e9, pex) so that the
existing-line qubits are activated by past instances of
three in a row. Next, we strongly couple l5 to w5, since
three in a row at move 5 is always a win. Finally, we
apply
PW (l5, l6, w5, w6, pwin),
PW (e7, l7, w6, w7, pwin),
PW (e8, l8, w7, w8, pwin),
and
PW (e9, l9, w8, w9, pwin)
gates to ensure that only the first three-in-a-row activates
the corresponding win qubit.
7) We wish to sample from games in which X wins, or games
in which O wins, or games ending in draws. In order to
achieve this, the degenerate ground state must be split
based on which player wins. To sample from states in
which X wins, we add a positive penalty pwb (for “win
bias”) to the biases of the victory qubits for moves on
which O could win, and a bonus −pwb to the biases for
the victory qubits representing X winning. Inverting these
penalties permits the opposite: sampling from paths that
give O the win. Adding the positive pwb penalty to victory
qubits for X and O results in sampling from the states
representing games that are draws.
The above permits tuning of the relative strengths of the
various penalties. For simplicity, we set pms = po = pline =
pnoline = pex = pwin = pwb = 1.
H. Choosing the next move based on quantum sampling
Given the above setup (or equivalent setup for any other
competitive game) that encodes the rules and win state for the
game, as well as any assumptions about how the computer’s
opponent will play (in our case, the assumption of minimally
strategic play), the general algorithm for strategic play is:
1) Using a quantum optimization algorithm, sample the
Hamiltonian for moves that lead to a win, loss, or draw,
carrying out a constant number of samples for each.
2) Given a set of sampled possible next moves M, for each
m ∈M, classically count nwin,m, nloss,m, and ndraw,m
(the number of future game paths that were sampled that
lead to a win, loss or draw for each candidate move m,
where wins, losses, and draws are read from the win,
line, and no line registers), as well as ntot,m = nwin,m +
nloss,m + ndraw,m and ntot = P

next move.

I. Quantum annealing hyperparameters
We carried out annealing runs on the DWave Advantage 2
System 1.13, performing 5 sets of 5,000 samples to sample
from the set of future game paths leading to each of wins,
losses, and draws (for a total of 75,000 samples per move;
see section II-G, rule 7, and section II-H). A separate minor
embedding for each set of 5,000 samples was found using the
minorminer algorithm [18]. The number of minorminer
attempts was increased to 2,048 from the default of 10, the
maximum number of failed iterations was increased to 256
from 10, chainlength patience was raised to 128 from 10, and
the timeout was set to 1,800 seconds.
J. Code availability
We implemented our tic-tac-toe-playing quantum computer
proof-of-principle using the D-Wave Ocean Python interface.

III. EARLY RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
We played games of tic-tac-toe against the algorithm de-
scribed in Section II executed on the D-Wave Advantage 2
System 1.13. We also allowed the quantum opponent to play
a randomly-moving classical opponent 60 times, with each
opponent starting 30 times. Across the 60 games, the average
number of logical qubits needed for modelling the future game
path from the ith move, including ancillary qubits, is shown
in Table IV. In later moves, there is some variation that arises
depending on the past moves chosen. The average number
of physical qubits to which this was mapped on the D-Wave
Advantage 2 system using the minorminer algorithm is also
shown. We found that the quantum opponent was always able
to defeat the random opponent when the former made the first
move, and was able to win in 26 out of 30 games (87% of the
time) when the random opponent started (Table V). No games
resulted in a draw. Since a competent human player can win
or force a draw every time, we did not collect win statistics
against a human.
As shown in Fig. 1, when the quantum annealer made the
first move, it produced noisy estimates of the win probabilities
of choosing a corner, edge, or centre square, but did correctly
determine the rank order. Since P ′ (win|m) ∝P (win|m),
we only expect rank order to match. However, even with

Qualitatively, the quantum opponent showed somewhat un-
even play, sometimes feeling like a real player capable of set-

obvious moves. Fig. 2A shows an example game against a
human player in which the quantum opponent exploited the

Although quantum annealing based sampling proved ade-
quate to win consistently against a random opponent when
the quantum player made the first move, some quirks were
apparent. The quantum player had no concept of a quick win
being more desirable than a slow one: in the game shown in
Fig. 2B, the quantum player had guaranteed a win for itself
after move 5, but rather than take the immediate win available
to it on move 7, it opted for the longer but equally inevitable
path to a win, something that most humans would not do.
Cases in which the random player won were cases in which
no winning path was open to the quantum annealer: since
our quantum strategy is currently configured to maximize win
probability and not to prefer draws to losses, the quantum
player ceased to pursue any particular strategy once a win
was impossible. An example of this is shown in Fig. 2C: at
move 6, no path can possibly lead to O (the quantum player)
winning, so it chooses the lowest-index square, which results
in a loss rather than a draw. This could be addressed with
minor adjustments to the classical outer part of the algorithm,
directing it to choose the move that minimizes P ′ (loss|m)
when quantum sampling yields P ′ (win|m) = 0 ∀m. We also
found that noisy sampling yielded few samples for particular
moves m sometimes, yielding to erroneously high estimates
of P ′ (win|m) in some cases when nwin,m and ntot,m were
both small. While lower-noise hardware should address this, a
practical classical workaround could be to add some arbitrary
positive constant to all nwin,m, nloss,m, and ndraw,m values,

IV. CONCLUSIONS
The work presented here represents an initial attempt to
program a quantum computer to play a competitive, traditional
game by considering all future game paths and by performing
unbiased sampling of these paths in order to identify the
next move that maximizes win probability. Although tic-tac-
toe is a very simple game, we were pleased to find that
current quantum annealers can consistently defeat a random
player. Extending this to more complex competitive games —
nim, Connect-Four, checkers, chess, Go, etc. — could inspire
quantum optimization algorithm advancements, and help to
benchmark quantum hardware. In principle, possible quantum
advantage within this setting stems from unbiased sampling
of the entire set of ground states (i.e., sampling from all future
game paths leading to a desired outcome, regardless how hard
to find they may be by classical algorithms). In practice,
embedding issues, noise, dynamic range limits, and other real-

all future game paths given the possible distribution of current
game states may be well-suited to quantum approaches. We
hope that game-playing quantum computers will help to make
quantum computing more understandable to laypeople.

Abstract: The challenge of programming classical computers to play traditional, competitive games against human players has helped to advance classical hardware and software. Quantum computers have the potential to play games in a unique way: programmed only with the rules of a game, they should be able to implicitly represent all future paths of a game leading to wins, losses, or draws, and sample from this path set to identify moves that maximize the likelihood of a win. This permits skilled play without hard-coded or machine-learned strategy. As a proof of principle, we present early results obtained after programming the D-Wave quantum annealer with the rules of tic-tac-toe, enabling it to play against a human opponent. We anticipate that, as it has for classical computers, game-playing will serve as an important real-world benchmark for quantum computers.
